entries.c606680ac7c4fdedd4ae44e849bcea54f88fbff4: <div sID="gen31257" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="1Cor.12" sID="1Cor.12"/> <div eID="gen31257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31258" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31259" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle, I. Considers the case of spiritual gifts, which were very plentifully poured out on the Corinthian church. He considers their original, that they are from God; their variety and use, that they were all intended for one and the same general end, the advancement of Christianity and the church's edification, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.1-Rom.12.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. He illustrates this by an allusion to a human body, in which all the members have a mutual relation and subserviency, and each has its proper place and use, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.12-Rom.12.26">ver. 12-26</reference>. III. He tells us that the church is the body of Christ, and the members are variously gifted for the benefit of the whole body, and each particular member, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.27-Rom.12.30">ver. 27-30</reference>. And them, IV. Closes with an exhortation to seek somewhat more beneficial than these gifts, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.31">ver. 31</reference>.
entries.8b1acf060560aa28070e84fc6d4acc754a1445bb: <div eID="gen31259" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31258" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">On Spiritual Gifts. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31260" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now concerning spiritual <hi type="italic">gifts,</hi> brethren, I would not have you ignorant. <hi type="super">2</hi> Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led. <hi type="super">3</hi> Wherefore I give you to understand, that no man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed: and <hi type="italic">that</hi> no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost. <hi type="super">4</hi> Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. <hi type="super">5</hi> And there are differences of administrations, but the same Lord. <hi type="super">6</hi> And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all. <hi type="super">7</hi> But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal. 8 For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit; <hi type="super">9</hi> To another faith by the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit; <hi type="super">10</hi> To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another <hi type="italic">divers</hi> kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues: <hi type="super">11</hi> But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will. <div eID="gen31260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31261" type="x-p"/> The apostle comes now to treat of spiritual gifts, which abounded in the church of Corinth, but were greatly abused. What these gifts were is at large told us in the body of the chapter; namely, extraordinary offices and powers, bestowed on ministers and Christians in the first ages, for conviction of unbelievers, and propagation of the gospel. Gifts and graces, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">charismata</hi></hi> and <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">charis,</hi></hi> greatly differ. Both indeed were freely given of God. But where grace is given it is for the salvation of those who have it. Gifts are bestowed for the advantage and salvation of others. And there may be great gifts where there is not a dram of grace, but persons possessed of them are utterly out of the divine favour. They are great instances of divine benignity to men, but do not by themselves prove those who have them to be the objects of divine complacency. This church was rich in gifts, but there were many things scandalously out of order in it. Now concerning these spiritual gifts, that is, the extraordinary powers they had received from the Spirit, <div eID="gen31261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31262" type="x-p"/> I. The apostle tells them he would not have them ignorant either of their original or use. They came from God, and were to be used for him. It would lead them far astray if they were ignorant of one or the other of these. Note, Right information is of great use as to all religious practice. It is wretched work which gifted men make who either do not know or do not advert to the nature and right use of the gifts with which they are endowed. <div eID="gen31262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31263" type="x-p"/> II. He puts them in the mind of the sad state out of which they had been recovered: <hi type="italic">You were Gentiles, carried away to dumb idols, even as you were led,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.12.2">v. 2</reference>. While they were so, they could have no pretensions to be spiritual men, nor to have spiritual gifts. While they were under the conduct of the spirit of Gentilism, they could not be influenced by the Spirit of Christ. If they well understood their former condition, they could not but know that all true spiritual gifts were from God. Now concerning this observe, 1. Their former character: they <hi type="italic">were Gentiles.</hi> Not God's peculiar people, but of the nations whom he had in a manner abandoned. The Jews were, before, his chosen people, distinguished from the rest of the world by his favour. To them the knowledge and worship of the true God were in a manner confined. The rest of the world were strangers to the covenant of promise, aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and in a manner without God, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Eph. ii. 12</reference>. Such Gentiles were the body of the Corinthians, before their conversion to Christianity. What a change was here! Christian Corinthians were once Gentiles. Note, It is of great use to the Christian, and a proper consideration to stir him up both to duty and thankfulness, to think what once he was: <hi type="italic">You were Gentiles.</hi> 2. The conduct they were under: <hi type="italic">Carried away to these dumb idols, even as you were led.</hi> They were hurried upon the grossest idolatry, the worship even of stocks and stones, through the force of a vain imagination, and the fraud of their priests practising on their ignorance, for, whatever were the sentiments of their philosophers, this was the practice of the herd. The body of the people paid their homage and worship to dumb idols, <hi type="italic">that had ears but could not hear, and mouths but could not speak,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.115.5-Ps.115.6">Ps. cxv. 5, 6</reference>. Miserable abjectness of mind! And those who despised these gross conceptions of the vulgar yet countenanced them by their practice. O dismal state of Gentilism! Could the Spirit of God be among such stupid idolators, or they be influenced by it? How did the prince of this world triumph in the blindness of mankind! How thick a mist had he cast over their minds! <div eID="gen31263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31264" type="x-p"/> III. He shows them how they might discern those gifts that were from the Spirit of God, true spiritual gifts: <hi type="italic">No man, speaking by the Spirit, calls Jesus accursed.</hi> Thus did both Jews and Gentiles: they blasphemed him as an impostor, and execrated his name, and deemed it abominable. And yet many Jews, who were exorcists and magicians, went about, pretending to work wonders by the Spirit of God (vid. Lightfoot's <hi type="italic">Horæ in loc.</hi>), and many among the Gentiles pretended to inspiration. Now the apostle tells them none could act under the influence, nor by the power, of the Spirit of God, who disowned and blasphemed Christ: for the Spirit of God bore uncontrollable witness to Christ by prophecy, miracles, his resurrection from the dead, the success of his doctrine among men, and its effect upon them; and could never so far contradict itself as to declare him accursed. And on the other hand <hi type="italic">no man could say Jesus was the Lord</hi> (that is, live by this faith, and work miracles to prove it), <hi type="italic">but it must be by the Holy Ghost.</hi> To own this truth before men, and maintain it to the death, and live under the influence of it, could not be done without the sanctification of the Holy Ghost. No man can call Christ <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> with a believing subjection to him and dependence upon him, unless that faith be wrought by the Holy Ghost. No man can confess this truth in the day of trial but by the Holy Ghost animating and encouraging him. Note, We have as necessary a dependence on the Spirit's operation and influence for our sanctification and perseverance as on the mediation of Christ for our reconciliation and acceptance with God: and no man could confirm this truth with a miracle but by the Holy Ghost. No evil spirit would lend assistance, if it were in his power, to spread a doctrine and religion so ruinous to the devil's kingdom. The substance of what the apostle asserts and argues here is that whatever pretences there were to inspiration or miracles, among those who were enemies to Christianity, they could not be from the Spirit of God; but no man could believe this with his heart, nor prove with a miracle that Jesus was Christ, but by the Holy Ghost: so that the extraordinary operations and powers among them did all proceed from the Spirit of God. He adds, <div eID="gen31264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31265" type="x-p"/> IV. These spiritual gifts, though proceeding from the same Spirit, are yet various. They have one author and original, but are themselves of various kinds. A free cause may produce variety of effects; and the same giver may bestow various gifts, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.4">v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">There are diversities of gifts,</hi> such as revelations, tongues, prophecy, interpretations of tongues; <hi type="italic">but the same Spirit.</hi> There are differences of administrations, or different offices, and officers to discharge them, different ordinances and institutions (see <reference osisRef="Rom.12.28-Rom.12.30">v. 28-30</reference>), but the same Lord, who appointed all, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.6">v. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">There are diversities of operations,</hi> or miraculous powers, called <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">energemata dynameon</hi></hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.10">v. 10</reference>), as here <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">energemata,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">but it is the same God that worketh all in all.</hi> There are various gifts, administrations, and operations, but all proceed from one God, one Lord, one Spirit; that is, from Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, the spring and origin of all spiritual blessings and bequests: all issue from the same fountain; all have the same author. However different they may be in themselves, in this they agree; all are from God. And several of the kinds are here specified, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.8-Rom.12.10">v. 8-10</reference>. Several persons had their several gifts, some one, some another, all from and by the same Spirit. To one was given the <hi type="italic">word of wisdom;</hi> that is, say some, a knowledge of the mysteries of the gospel, and ability to explain them, an exact understanding of the design, nature, and doctrines, of the Christian religion. Others say an uttering of grave sentences, like Solomon's proverbs. Some confine this word of wisdom to the revelations made to and by the apostles.—<hi type="italic">To another the word of knowledge, by the same Spirit;</hi> that is, say some, the knowledge of mysteries (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.13">ch. ii. 13</reference>): wrapped up in the prophecies, types, and histories of the Old Testament: say others, a skill and readiness to give advice and counsel in perplexed cases.—<hi type="italic">To another faith, by the same Spirit;</hi> that is, the faith of miracles, or a faith in the divine power and promise, whereby they were enabled to trust God in any emergency, and go on in the way of their duty, and own and profess the truths of Christ, whatever was the difficulty or danger.—<hi type="italic">To another the gift of healing, by the same Spirit;</hi> that is, healing the sick, either by laying on of hands, or anointing with oil, or with a bare word.—<hi type="italic">To another the working of miracles;</hi> the efficacies of powers, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">energemata dynameon,</hi></hi> such as raising the dead, restoring the blind to sight, giving speech to the dumb, hearing to the deaf, and the use of limbs to the lame.—<hi type="italic">To another prophecy,</hi> that is, ability to foretel future events, which is the more usual sense of prophecy; or to explain scripture by a peculiar gift of the Spirit. See <reference osisRef="Rom.14.24">ch. xiv. 24</reference>.—<hi type="italic">To another the discerning of Spirits,</hi> power to distinguish between true and false prophets, or to discern the real and internal qualifications of any person for an office, or to discover the inward workings of the mind by the Holy Ghost, as Peter did those of Ananias, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.3">Acts v. 3</reference>.—<hi type="italic">To another divers kinds of tongues,</hi> or ability to speak languages by inspiration.—<hi type="italic">To another the interpretation of tongues,</hi> or ability to render foreign languages readily and properly into their own. With such variety of spiritual gifts were the first ministers and churches blessed. <div eID="gen31265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31266" type="x-p"/> V. The end for which these gifts were bestowed: <hi type="italic">The manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.12.7">v. 7</reference>. The Spirit was manifested by the exercise of these gifts; his influence and interest appeared in them. But they were not distributed for the mere honour and advantage of those who had them, but for the benefit of the church, to edify the body, and spread and advance the gospel. Note, Whatever gifts God confers on any man, he confers them that he may do good with them, whether they be common or spiritual. The outward gifts of his bounty are to be improved for his glory, and employed in doing good to others. No man has them merely for himself. They are a trust put into his hands, to profit withal; and the more he profits others with them, the more abundantly will they turn to his account in the end, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.17">Phil. iv. 17</reference>. Spiritual gifts are bestowed, that men may with them profit the church and promote Christianity. They are not given for show, but for service; not for pomp and ostentation, but for edification; not to magnify those that have them, but to edify others. <div eID="gen31266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31267" type="x-p"/> VI. The measure and proportion in which they are given: <hi type="italic">All these worketh one and the same Spirit, dividing to every man as he will.</hi> It is according to the sovereign pleasure of the donor. What more free than a gift? And shall not the Spirit of God do what he will with his own? May he not give to what persons he pleases, and in what proportion he pleases; one gift to one man, and another to another; to one more, and another fewer, as he thinks fit? Is he not the best judge how his own purpose shall be served, and his own donatives bestowed? It is not as men will, nor as they may think fit, but as the Spirit pleases. Note, The Holy Ghost is a divine person. He works divine effects and divides divine gifts a he will, by his own power, and according to his own pleasure, without dependence or control. But though he distributes these gifts freely and uncontrollably, they are intended by him, not for private honour and advantage, but for public benefit, for the edification of the body, the church.
entries.8be0e580527d56f429ab33711091c11dcdcb6bdd: <div eID="gen31267" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Union Recommended. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31268" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also <hi type="italic">is</hi> Christ. <hi type="super">13</hi> For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether <hi type="italic">we be</hi> Jews or Gentiles, whether <hi type="italic">we be</hi> bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit. <hi type="super">14</hi> For the body is not one member, but many. <hi type="super">15</hi> If the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body? <hi type="super">16</hi> And if the ear shall say, Because I am not the eye, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body? <hi type="super">17</hi> If the whole body <hi type="italic">were</hi> an eye, where <hi type="italic">were</hi> the hearing? If the whole <hi type="italic">were</hi> hearing, where <hi type="italic">were</hi> the smelling? <hi type="super">18</hi> But now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him. <hi type="super">19</hi> And if they were all one member, where <hi type="italic">were</hi> the body? <hi type="super">20</hi> But now <hi type="italic">are they</hi> many members, yet but one body. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you. <hi type="super">22</hi> Nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary: <hi type="super">23</hi> And those <hi type="italic">members</hi> of the body, which we think to be less honourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour; and our uncomely <hi type="italic">parts</hi> have more abundant comeliness. <hi type="super">24</hi> For our comely <hi type="italic">parts</hi> have no need: but God hath tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that <hi type="italic">part</hi> which lacked: <hi type="super">25</hi> That there should be no schism in the body; but <hi type="italic">that</hi> the members should have the same care one for another. <hi type="super">26</hi> And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it. <div eID="gen31268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31269" type="x-p"/> The apostle here makes out the truth of what was above asserted, and puts the gifted men among the Corinthians in mind of their duty, by comparing the church of Christ to a human body. <div eID="gen31269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31270" type="x-p"/> I. By telling us that one body may have many members, and that the many members of the same body make but one body (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">As the body is one, and hath many members, and all members of that one body, being many, are one body, so also is Christ;</hi> that is, Christ mystical, as divines commonly speak. Christ and his church making one body, as head and members, this body is made up of many parts or members, yet but one body; for all the members are <hi type="italic">baptized into the same body, and made to drink of the same Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.12.13">v. 13</reference>. Jews and Gentiles, bond and free, are upon a level in this: all are baptized into the same body, and made partakers of the same Spirit. Christians become members of this body by baptism: they are baptized into one body. The outward rite is of divine institution, significant of the new birth, called therefore <hi type="italic">the washing of regeneration,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">Tit. iii. 5</reference>. But it is by the Spirit, by the renewing of the Holy Ghost, that we are made members of Christ's body. It is the Spirit's operation, signified by the outward administration, that makes us members. And by communion at the other ordinance we are sustained; but then it is not merely by drinking the wine, but by drinking into one Spirit. The outward administration is a means appointed of God for our participation in this great benefit; but it is baptism by the Spirit, it is internal renovation and drinking into one Spirit, partaking of his sanctifying influence from time to time, that makes us true members of Christ's body, and maintains our union with him. Being animated by one Spirit makes Christians one body. Note, All who have the spirit of Christ, without difference, are the members of Christ, whether Jew or Gentile, bond or free; and none but such. And all the members of Christ make up one body; the members many, but the body one. They are one body, because they have one principle of life; all are quickened and animated by the same Spirit. <div eID="gen31270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31271" type="x-p"/> II. Each member has its particular form, place, and use. 1. The meanest member makes a part of the body. The foot and ear are less useful, perhaps, than the hand and eye; but because one is not a hand, and the other an eye, shall they say, therefore, that they do not belong to the body? <reference osisRef="Rom.12.15-Rom.12.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. So every member of the body mystical cannot have the same place and office; but what then? Shall it hereupon disown relation to the body? Because it is not fixed in the same station, or favoured with the same gifts as others, shall it say, "I do not belong to Christ?" No, the meanest member of his body is as much a member as the noblest, and as truly regarded by him. All his members are dear to him. 2. There must be a distinction of members in the body: <hi type="italic">Were the whole body eye, where were the hearing? Were the whole ear, where were the smelling?</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.12.17">v. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">If all were one member, where were the body?</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.12.19">v. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">They are many members,</hi> and for that reason must have distinction among them, <hi type="italic">and yet are but one body,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.12.20">v. 20</reference>. One member of a body is not a body; this is made up of many; and among these many there must be a distinction, difference of situation, shape, use, &c. So it is in the body of Christ; its members must have different uses, and therefore have different powers, and be in different places, some having one gift, and others a different one. Variety in the members of the body contributes to the beauty of it. What a monster would a body be if it were all ear, or eye, or arm! So it is for the beauty and good appearance of the church that there should be diversity of gifts and offices in it. 3. The disposal of members in a natural body, and their situation, are as God pleases: <hi type="italic">But now hath God set the members, every one of them, in the body, as it hath pleased him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.12.18">v. 18</reference>. We may plainly perceive the divine wisdom in the distribution of the members; but it was made according to the counsel of his will; he distinguished and distributed them as he pleased. So is it also in the members of Christ's body: they are chosen out to such stations, and endued with such gifts, as God pleases. He who is sovereign Lord of all disposes his favours and gifts as he will. And who should gainsay his pleasure? What foundation is here for repining in ourselves, or envying others? We should be doing the duties of our own place, and not murmuring in ourselves, nor quarrelling with others, that we are not in theirs. 4. All the members of the body are, in some respect, useful and necessary to each other: <hi type="italic">The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of thee; nor the head to the feet, I have no need of your:</hi> nay, those members of the body <hi type="italic">which seem to be more feeble</hi> (the bowels, &c.) <hi type="italic">are necessary</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.21-Rom.12.22">v. 21, 22</reference>); God has so fitted and tempered them together that they are all necessary to one another, and to the whole body; there is no part redundant and unnecessary. Every member serves some good purpose or other: it is useful to its fellow-members, and necessary to the good state of the whole body. Nor is there a member of the body of Christ but may and ought to be useful to his fellow-members, and at some times, and in some cases, is needful to them. None should despise and envy another, seeing God has made the distinction between them as he pleased, yet so as to keep them all in some degree of mutual dependence, and make them valuable to each other, and concerned for each other, because of their mutual usefulness. Those who excel in any gift cannot say that they have no need of those who in that gift are their inferiors, while perhaps, in other gifts, they exceed them. Nay, the lowest members of all have their use, and the highest cannot do well without them. The eye has need of the hand, and the head of the feet. 5. Such is the man's concern for his whole body that <hi type="italic">on the less honourable members more abundant honour is bestowed, and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness.</hi> Those parts which are not fit, like the rest, to be exposed to view, which are either deformed or shameful, we most carefully clothe and cover; whereas the comely parts have no such need. The wisdom of Providence has so contrived and tempered things that the most abundant regard and honour should be paid to that which most wanted it, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.24">v. 24</reference>. So should the members of Christ's body behave towards their fellow-members: instead of despising them, or reproaching them, for their infirmities, they should endeavour to cover and conceal them, and put the best face upon them that they can. 6. Divine wisdom has contrived and ordered things in this manner that the members of the body should not be schismatics, divided from each other and acting upon separate interests, but well affected to each other, tenderly concerned for each other, having a fellow-feeling of each other's griefs and a communion in each other's pleasures and joys, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.25-Rom.12.26">v. 25, 26</reference>. God has tempered the members of the body natural in the manner mentioned, that <hi type="italic">there might be no schism in the body</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.25">v. 25</reference>), no rupture nor disunion among the members, nor so much as the least mutual disregard. This should be avoided also in the spiritual body of Christ. There should be no schism in this body, but the members should be closely united by the strongest bonds of love. All decays of this affection are the seeds of schism. Where Christians grow cold towards each other, they will be careless and unconcerned for each other. And this mutual disregard is a schism begun. The members of the natural body are made to have a care and concern for each other, to prevent a schism in it. So should it be in Christ's body; the members should sympathize with each other. As in the natural body the pain of the one part afflicts the whole, the ease and pleasure of one part affects the whole, so should Christians reckon themselves honoured in the honours of their fellow-christians, and should suffer in their sufferings. Note, Christian sympathy is a great branch of Christian duty. We should be so far from slighting our brethren's sufferings that we should suffer with them, so far from envying their honours that we should rejoice with them and reckon ourselves honoured in them.
entries.fde6dbf8f03c2794fd79de5f355fc82aae8003e7: <div eID="gen31271" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">On Spiritual Gifts. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31272" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular. <hi type="super">28</hi> And God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues. <hi type="super">29</hi> <hi type="italic">Are</hi> all apostles? <hi type="italic">are</hi> all prophets? <hi type="italic">are</hi> all teachers? <hi type="italic">are</hi> all workers of miracles? <hi type="super">30</hi> Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues? do all interpret? <hi type="super">31</hi> But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet show I unto you a more excellent way. <div eID="gen31272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31273" type="x-p"/> I. Here the apostle sums up the argument, and applies this similitude to the church of Christ, concerning which observe, <div eID="gen31273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31274" type="x-p"/> 1. The relation wherein Christians stand to Christ and one another. The church, or whole collective body of Christians, in all ages, is his body. Every Christian is a member of his body, and every other Christian stands related to him as a fellow-member (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Now you are the body of Christ, and members in particular,</hi> or particular members. Each is a member of the body, not the whole body; each stands related to the body as a part of it, and all have a common relation to one another, dependence upon one another, and should have a mutual care and concern. Thus are the members of the natural body, thus should the members of the mystical body be, disposed. Note, Mutual indifference, and much more contempt, and hatred, and envy, and strife, are very unnatural in Christians. It is like the members of the same body being destitute of all concern for one another, or quarrelling with each other. This is the apostle's scope in this argument. He endeavours in it to suppress the proud, vaunting, and contentious spirit, that had prevailed among the Corinthians, by reason of their spiritual gifts. <div eID="gen31274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31275" type="x-p"/> 2. The variety of offices instituted by Christ, and gifts or favours dispensed by him (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">God hath set some in the church; first, apostles,</hi> the chief ministers entrusted with all the powers necessary to found a church, and make an entire revelation of God's will. <hi type="italic">Secondarily, prophets,</hi> or persons enabled by inspiration, as the evangelists did. <hi type="italic">Thirdly, teachers,</hi> those who labour in word and doctrine, whether with pastoral charge or without it. After that, <hi type="italic">miracles,</hi> or miracle-workers. <hi type="italic">The gifts of healing,</hi> or those who had power to heal diseases; <hi type="italic">helps,</hi> or such as had compassion on the sick and weak, and ministered to them; <hi type="italic">governments,</hi> or such as had the disposal of the charitable contributions of the church, and dealt them out to the poor; <hi type="italic">diversities of tongues,</hi> or such as could speak divers languages. Concerning all these observe, (1.) The plenteous variety of these gifts and offices. What a multitude are they! A good God was free in his communications to the primitive church; he was no niggard of his benefits and favours. No, he provided richly for them. They had no want, but a store-all that was necessary, and even more; what was convenient for them too. (2.) Observe the order of these offices and gifts. They are here placed in their proper ranks. Those of most value have the first place. Apostles, prophets, and teachers, were all intended to instruct the people, to inform them well in the things of God, and promote their spiritual edification: without them, neither evangelical knowledge nor holiness could have been promoted. But the rest, however fitted to answer the great intentions of Christianity, had no such immediate regard to religion, strictly so called. Note, God does, and we should, value things according to their real worth: and the use of things is the best criterion of their real worth. Those are most valuable that best answer the highest purposes. Such were apostolical powers, compared with theirs who had only the gift of healing and miracles. What holds the last and lowest rank in this enumeration is diversity of tongues. It is by itself the most useless and insignificant of all these gifts. Healing diseases, relieving the poor, helping the sick, have their use: but how vain a thing is it to speak languages, if a man does it merely to amuse or boast himself! This may indeed raise the admiration, but cannot promote the edification, of the hearers, nor do them any good. And yet it is manifest from <reference osisRef="Rom.14.1-Rom.14.23">ch. xiv.</reference> that the Corinthians valued themselves exceedingly on this gift. Note, How proper a method it is to beat down pride to let persons know the true value of what they pride themselves in! It is but too common a thing for men to value themselves most on what is least worth: and it is of great use to bring them to a sober mind by letting them know how much they are mistaken. (3.) The various distribution of these gifts, not all to one, nor to every one alike. All members and officers had not the same rank in the church, nor the same endowments (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.29-Rom.12.30">v. 29, 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">Are all apostles? Are all prophets?</hi> This were to make the church a monster: all one as if the body were all ear or all eye. Some are fit for one office and employment, and some for another; and the Spirit distributes to every one as he will. We must be content with our own rank and share, if they be lower and less than those of others. We must not be conceited of ourselves, and despise others, if we are in the higher rank and have greater gifts. Every member of the body is to preserve its own rank, and do its own office; and all are to minister to one another, and promote the good of the body in general, without envying, or despising, or neglecting, or ill-using, any one particular member. How blessed a constitution were the Christian church, if all the members did their duty! <div eID="gen31275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31276" type="x-p"/> II. He closes this chapter with an advice (as the generality read it) and a hint. 1. An advice to covet the best gifts, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">charismata ta kreittona</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">dona potiora, præstantiora,</hi> either the most valuable in them selves or the most serviceable to others; and these are, in truth, most valuable in themselves, though men may be apt to esteem those most that will raise their fame and esteem highest. Those are truly best by which God will be most honoured and his church edified. Such gifts should be most earnestly coveted. Note, We should desire that most which is best, and most worth. Grace is therefore to be preferred before gifts; and, of gifts, those are to be preferred which are of greatest use. But some read this passage, not as an advice, but a charge: <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">zeloute,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">You are envious</hi> at each other's gifts. In <reference osisRef="Rom.13.4">ch. xiii. 4</reference>, the same word is thus translated. You quarrel and contend about them. This they certainly did. And this behaviour the apostle here reprehends, and labours to rectify. <hi type="italic">Only of pride cometh contention.</hi> These contests in the church of Corinth sprang from this original. It was a quarrel about precedency (as most quarrels among Christians are, with whatever pretences they are gilded over); and it is no wonder that a quarrel about precedence should extinguish charity. When all would stand in the first rank, no wonder if they jostle, or throw down, or thrust back, their brethren. Gifts may be valued for their use, but they are mischievous when made the fuel of pride and contention. This therefore the apostle endeavours to prevent. 2. By giving them the hint of a more excellent way, namely, of charity, of mutual love and good-will. This was the only right way to quiet and cement them, and make their gifts turn to the advantage and edification of the church. This would render them kind to each other, and concerned for each other, and therefore calm their spirits, and put an end to their little piques and contests, their disputes about precedency. Those would appear to be in the foremost rank, according to the apostle, who had most of true Christian love. Note, True charity is greatly to be preferred to the most glorious gifts. To have the heart glow with mutual love is vastly better than to glare with the most pompous titles, offices, or powers.  <chapter eID="1Cor.12"/> <div eID="gen31276" type="x-p"/>

entries.56a31897f61df3a6181beeed4fd0d5864671c6a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17006"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <div sID="gen33632" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.1-1Cor.12.31">1Co 12:1-31</reference>. The Use and the Abuse of Spiritual Gifts, Especially Prophesying and Tongues.<div eID="gen33632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33633" type="x-p"/> This is the second subject for correction in the Corinthian assemblies: the "first" was discussed (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.18-1Cor.11.34">1Co 11:18-34</reference>).<div eID="gen33633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33634" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17006"/><hi type="bold">1. spiritual gifts--</hi>the signs of the Spirit's continued efficacious presence in the Church, which is Christ's body, the complement of His incarnation, as the body is the complement of the head. By the love which pervades the whole, the gifts of the several members, forming reciprocal complements to each other, tend to the one object of perfecting the body of Christ. The ordinary and permanent gifts are comprehended together with the extraordinary, without distinction specified, as both alike flow from the divine indwelling Spirit of life. The extraordinary gifts, so far from making professors more peculiarly saints than in our day, did not always even prove that such persons were in a safe state at all (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.22">Mt 7:22</reference>). They were needed at first in the Church: (1) as a pledge to Christians themselves who had just passed over from Judaism or heathendom, that God was in the Church; (2) for the propagation of Christianity in the world; (3) for the edification of the Church. Now that we have the whole written New Testament (which they had not) and Christianity established as the result of the miracles, we need no further miracle to attest the truth. So the pillar of cloud which guided the Israelites was withdrawn when they were sufficiently assured of the Divine Presence, the manifestation of God's glory being thenceforward enclosed in the Most Holy Place [Archbishop Whately]. Paul sets forth in order: (1). The unity of the body (1Co 12:1-27). (2). The variety of its members and functions (1Co 12:27-30). (3). The grand principle for the right exercise of the gifts, namely, love (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.31">1Co 12:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1-1Cor.13.4">1Co 13:1-13). (4</reference>) The comparison of the gifts with one another (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1-1Cor.14.40">1Co 14:1-40</reference>).<div eID="gen33634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I would not have you ignorant--</hi>with all your boasts of "knowledge" at Corinth. If ignorant now, it will be your own fault, not mine (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.38">1Co 14:38</reference>). <div eID="gen33635" type="x-p"/>
entries.87798ecb5a69553f4790493e2a9ee3e5bd4e95a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17007"/><div sID="gen33636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17007"/>2. (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.11">Ep 2:11</reference>).<div eID="gen33636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33637" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that ye were--</hi>The best manuscripts read, "That WHEN ye were"; thus "ye were" must be supplied before "carried away"--Ye were blindly transported hither and thither at the will of your false guides.<div eID="gen33637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">these dumb idols--</hi>Greek, "the idols which are dumb"; contrasted with the living God who "speaks" in the believer by His Spirit (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1Co 12:3</reference>, &c.). This gives the reason why the Corinthians needed instruction as to spiritual gifts, namely, their past heathen state, wherein they had no experience of intelligent spiritual powers. When blind, ye went to the dumb.<div eID="gen33638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33639" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ye were led--</hi>The Greek is, rather, "as ye might (happen to) be led," namely, on different occasions. The heathen oracles led their votaries at random, without any definite principle. <div eID="gen33639" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7cc99e99ba83065ce0fb5e4466605653ed3af22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17008"/><div sID="gen33640" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17008"/><hi type="bold">3. The negative and positive criteria of inspiration by the Spirit--</hi>the rejection or confession of Jesus as Lord [Alford] (<reference osisRef="1John.4.2">1Jo 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.1">5:1</reference>). Paul gives a test of truth against the Gentiles; John, against the false prophets.<div eID="gen33640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33641" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the Spirit--</hi>rather, as Greek, "IN the Spirit"; that being the power pervading him, and the element in which he speaks [Alford], (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.17">Mt 16:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.26">Joh 15:26</reference>).<div eID="gen33641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God ... Holy--</hi>The same Spirit is called at one time "the Spirit of God"; at another, "the HOLY Ghost," or "Holy Spirit." Infinite Holiness is almost synonymous with Godhead.<div eID="gen33642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speaking ... say--</hi>"Speak" implies the act of utterance; "say" refers to that which is uttered. Here, "say" means a spiritual and believing confession of Him.<div eID="gen33643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33644" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus--</hi>not an abstract doctrine, but the historical, living God-man (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.9">Ro 10:9</reference>).<div eID="gen33644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33645" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">accursed--</hi>as the Jews and Gentiles treated Him (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">Ga 3:13</reference>). Compare "to curse Christ" in the heathen Pliny's letter [Epistles, 10.97]. The spiritual man feels Him to be the Source of all blessings (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Ep 1:3</reference>) and to be severed from Him is to be accursed (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.3">Ro 9:3</reference>).<div eID="gen33645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33646" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord--</hi>acknowledging himself as His servant (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.13">Is 26:13</reference>). "Lord" is the Septuagint translation for the incommunicable Hebrew name Jehovah. <div eID="gen33646" type="x-p"/>
entries.0eb8ccafe84fb13379315c41b7114172b6ce75a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17009"/><div sID="gen33647" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17009"/><hi type="bold">4. diversities of gifts--</hi>that is, varieties of spiritual endowments peculiar to the several members of the Church: compare "dividing to every man severally" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.11">1Co 12:11</reference>).<div eID="gen33647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33648" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">same Spirit--</hi>The Holy Trinity appears here: the Holy Spirit in this verse; Christ in <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.5">1Co 12:5</reference>; and the Father in <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.6">1Co 12:6</reference>. The terms "gifts," "administrations," and "operations," respectively correspond to the Divine Three. The Spirit is treated of in <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.7">1Co 12:7</reference>, &c.; the Lord, in <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.12">1Co 12:12</reference>, &c.; God, in <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.28">1Co 12:28</reference>. (Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.4-Eph.4.6">Ep 4:4-6</reference>). <div eID="gen33648" type="x-p"/>
entries.f67e3f9282053d9f47e8943663810095e975c825: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17010"/><div sID="gen33649" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17010"/>5-6. "Gifts" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4">1Co 12:4</reference>), "administrations" (the various functions and services performed by those having the gifts, compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.28">1Co 12:28</reference>), and "operations" (the actual effects resulting from both the former, through the universally operative power of the one Father who is "above all, through all, and in us all"), form an ascending climax [Henderson, Inspiration].<div eID="gen33649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33650" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">same Lord--</hi>whom the Spirit glorifies by these ministrations [Bengel]. <div eID="gen33650" type="x-p"/>
entries.8389e7d4716298983eae2d122be224b737d98c2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17012"/><div sID="gen33654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17012"/><hi type="bold">7. But--</hi>Though all the gifts flow from the one God, Lord, and Spirit, the "manifestation" by which the Spirit acts (as He is hidden in Himself), varies in each individual.<div eID="gen33654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to every man--</hi>to each of the members of the Church severally.<div eID="gen33655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to profit withal--</hi>with a view to the profit of the whole body. <div eID="gen33656" type="x-p"/>
entries.5529032917bfef776c52ca1afc6dd6f8e860885c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17013"/><div sID="gen33657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17013"/>8-10. Three classes of gifts are distinguished by a distinct Greek word for "another" (a distinct class), marking the three several genera: allo marks the species, hetero the genera (compare Greek, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.39-1Cor.15.41">1Co 15:39-41</reference>). I. Gifts of intellect, namely, (1) wisdom; (2) knowledge. II. Gifts dependent on a special faith, namely, that of miracles (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.20">Mt 17:20</reference>): (1) healings; (2) workings of miracles; (3) prophecy of future events; (4) discerning of spirits, or the divinely given faculty of distinguishing between those really inspired, and those who pretended to inspiration. III. Gifts referring to the tongues: (1) diverse kinds of tongues; (2) interpretation of tongues. The catalogue in <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.28">1Co 12:28</reference> is not meant strictly to harmonize with the one here, though there are some particulars in which they correspond. The three genera are summarily referred to by single instances of each in <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.8">1Co 13:8</reference>. The first genus refers more to believers; the second, to unbelievers.<div eID="gen33657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by ... by ... by--</hi>The first in Greek is, "By means of," or "through the operation of"; the second is, "according to" the disposing of (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.11">1Co 12:11</reference>); the third is, "in," that is, under the influence of (so the Greek, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.43">Mt 22:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.27">Lu 2:27</reference>).<div eID="gen33658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">word of wisdom--</hi>the ready utterance of (for imparting to others, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>) wisdom, namely, new revelations of the divine wisdom in redemption, as contrasted with human philosophy (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.24">1Co 1:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.7">2:6, 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.8">Ep 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.10">3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.3">Col 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen33659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33660" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">word of knowledge--</hi>ready utterance supernaturally imparted of truths ALREADY REVEALED (in this it is distinguished from "the word of wisdom," which related to NEW revelations). Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.6">1Co 14:6</reference>, where "revelation" (answering to "wisdom" here) is distinguished from "knowledge" [Henderson]. Wisdom or revelation belonged to the "prophets"; knowledge, to the "teachers." Wisdom penetrates deeper than knowledge. Knowledge relates to things that are to be done. Wisdom, to things eternal: hence, wisdom is not, like knowledge, said to "pass away" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.8">1Co 13:8</reference>), [Bengel]. <div eID="gen33660" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce7b79afa9a72572c9f8251655a0befcd8c111c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17016"/><div sID="gen33668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17016"/><hi type="bold">11. as he will--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.18">1Co 12:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.4">He 2:4</reference>). <div eID="gen33668" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1c676c67a2c31d4fc054e44a19583c04e6ac059: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17017"/><div sID="gen33669" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17017"/>12-13. Unity, not unvarying uniformity, is the law of God in the world of grace, as in that of nature. As the many members of the body compose an organic whole and none can be dispensed with as needless, so those variously gifted by the Spirit, compose a spiritual organic whole, the body of Christ, into which all are baptized by the one Spirit.<div eID="gen33669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of that one body--</hi>Most of the oldest manuscripts omit "one."<div eID="gen33670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so also is Christ--</hi>that is, the whole Christ, the head and body. So <reference osisRef="Ps.18.50">Psa 18:50</reference>, "His anointed (Messiah or Christ), David (the antitypical David) and His seed." <div eID="gen33671" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b52e7916d56844451e53b2752a8c43f98bf156c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17019"/><div sID="gen33676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17019"/>14. Translate, "For the body also." The analogy of the body, not consisting exclusively of one, but of many members, illustrates the mutual dependence of the various members in the one body, the Church. The well-known fable of the belly and the other members, spoken by Menenius Agrippa, to the seceding commons [Livy, 2.32], was probably before Paul's mind, stored as it was with classical literature. <div eID="gen33676" type="x-p"/>
entries.acd3338e3c7532bb293b2ff56c1f530f27223862: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17020"/><div sID="gen33677" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17020"/>15. The humbler members ought not to disparage themselves, or to be disparaged by others more noble (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.21">1Co 12:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen33677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foot ... hand--</hi>The humble speaks of the more honorable member which most nearly resembles itself: so the "ear" of the "eye" (the nobler and more commanding member, <reference osisRef="Num.10.31">Nu 10:31</reference>), (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.16">1Co 12:16</reference>). As in life each compares himself with those whom he approaches nearest in gifts, not those far superior. The foot and hand represent men of active life; the ear and eye, those of contemplative life. <div eID="gen33678" type="x-p"/>
entries.01338a0d5d0dd6ce7d2d8d0b16d93a6a63049652: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17021"/><div sID="gen33679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17021"/>17. Superior as the eye is, it would not do if it were the sole member to the exclusion of the rest. <div eID="gen33679" type="x-p"/>
entries.678424ff744aefc56d52c368148b6220deac70c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17022"/><div sID="gen33680" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17022"/><hi type="bold">18. now--</hi>as the case really is.<div eID="gen33680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every one--</hi>each severally. <div eID="gen33681" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4ea59613d1e2985697236e00a49cddb4a1313d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17023"/><div sID="gen33682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17023"/><hi type="bold">19. where were the body--</hi>which, by its very idea, "hath many members" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.12">1Co 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.14">14</reference>), [Alford]. <div eID="gen33682" type="x-p"/>
entries.91568dfef8cdffd1e403806f292b304d6e03fa9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17024"/><div sID="gen33683" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17024"/><hi type="bold">20. now--</hi>as the case really is: in contrast to the supposition (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.19">1Co 12:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.18">1Co 12:18</reference>).<div eID="gen33683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">many members--</hi>mutually dependent. <div eID="gen33684" type="x-p"/>
entries.e79016732f3b83547b306714c839c6bd3d92056c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17025"/><div sID="gen33685" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17025"/>21. The higher cannot dispense with the lower members. <div eID="gen33685" type="x-p"/>
entries.a52dd8c9316f5f12b1261e64e80fc342fb71a241: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17026"/><div sID="gen33686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17026"/><hi type="bold">22. more feeble--</hi>more susceptible of injury: for example, the brain, the belly, the eye. Their very feebleness, so far from doing away with the need for them, calls forth our greater care for their preservation, as being felt "necessary." <div eID="gen33686" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe069937e9fcc0c716cb26253a1390783e625580: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17027"/><div sID="gen33687" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17027"/><hi type="bold">23. less honourable--</hi>"We think" the feet and the belly "less honorable," though not really so in the nature of things.<div eID="gen33687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bestow ... honour--</hi>putting shoes on (Margin) the feet, and clothes to cover the belly.<div eID="gen33688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uncomely parts--</hi>the secret parts: the poorest, though unclad in the rest of the body, cover these. <div eID="gen33689" type="x-p"/>
entries.32f2cdc6080f489f2163e90260aea1c8a3a89c6c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17028"/><div sID="gen33690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17028"/><hi type="bold">24. tempered ... together--</hi>on the principle of mutual compensation.<div eID="gen33690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33691" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to that part which lacked--</hi>to the deficient part [Alford], (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.23">1Co 12:23</reference>). <div eID="gen33691" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d8c6fa2595a2387578de6327ed178ed4b5ef320: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17029"/><div sID="gen33692" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17029"/><hi type="bold">25. no schism--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.21">1Co 12:21</reference>)--no disunion; referring to the "divisions" noticed (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.18">1Co 11:18</reference>).<div eID="gen33692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33693" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">care one for another--</hi>that is, in behalf of one another. <div eID="gen33693" type="x-p"/>
entries.ade6e08194a32c47cfbccf5059c0cd71c56bbeef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17030"/><div sID="gen33694" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17030"/><hi type="bold">26. And--</hi>Accordingly.<div eID="gen33694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... suffer with it--</hi>"When a thorn enters the heel, the whole body feels it, and is concerned: the back bends, the belly and thighs contract themselves, the hands come forward and draw out the thorn, the head stoops, and the eyes regard the affected member with intense gaze" [Chrysostom].<div eID="gen33695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoice with it--</hi>"When the head is crowned, the whole man feels honored, the mouth expresses, and the eyes look, gladness" [Chrysostom]. <div eID="gen33696" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc7a9ca1a33455063cb33e9379468247d42c3d82: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17031"/><div sID="gen33697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17031"/><hi type="bold">27. members in particular--</hi>that is, severally members of it. Each church is in miniature what the whole aggregate of churches is collectively, "the body of Christ" (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.16">1Co 3:16</reference>): and its individual components are members, every one in his assigned place. <div eID="gen33697" type="x-p"/>
entries.3da00d19d5768280cb33ab9e00cbcacb6471d4a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17032"/><div sID="gen33698" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17032"/><hi type="bold">28. set ... in the church--</hi>as He has "set the members ... in the body" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.18">1Co 12:18</reference>).<div eID="gen33698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">first apostles--</hi>above even the prophets. Not merely the Twelve, but others are so called, for example, Barnabas, &c. (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.7">Ro 16:7</reference>).<div eID="gen33699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33700" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">teachers--</hi>who taught, for the most part, truths already revealed; whereas the prophets made new revelations and spoke all their prophesyings under the Spirit's influence. As the teachers had the "word of knowledge," so the prophets "the word of wisdom" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.8">1Co 12:8</reference>). Under "teachers" are included "evangelists and pastors."<div eID="gen33700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">miracles--</hi>literally, "powers" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.10">1Co 12:10</reference>): ranked below "teachers," as the function of teaching is more edifying, though less dazzling than working miracles.<div eID="gen33701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">helps, governments--</hi>lower and higher departments of "ministrations" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.5">1Co 12:5</reference>); as instances of the former, deacons whose office it was to help in the relief of the poor, and in baptizing and preaching, subordinate to higher ministers (Ac 6:1-10; 8:5-17); also, others who helped with their time and means, in the Lord's cause (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.13">1Co 13:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.11.17">Nu 11:17</reference>). The Americans similarly use "helps" for "helpers." And, as instances of the latter, presbyters, or bishops, whose office it was to govern the Church (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1Ti 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">He 13:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.24">24</reference>). These officers, though now ordinary and permanent, were originally specially endowed with the Spirit for their office, whence they are here classified with other functions of an inspired character. Government (literally, "guiding the helm" of affairs), as being occupied with external things, notwithstanding the outward status it gives, is ranked by the Spirit with the lower functions. Compare "He that giveth" (answering to "helps")--"he that ruleth" (answering to "governments") (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.8">Ro 12:8</reference>). Translate, literally, "Helpings, governings" [Alford].<div eID="gen33702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">diversities of tongues--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.10">1Co 12:10</reference>). "Divers kinds of tongues." <div eID="gen33703" type="x-p"/>
entries.528fb98d57c64858f3218ddc072705ebc8187ac0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17033"/><div sID="gen33704" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17033"/><hi type="bold">29. Are all?--</hi>Surely not. <div eID="gen33704" type="x-p"/>
entries.c59299294b692ff4a656f8da80441159901bb402: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17034"/><div sID="gen33705" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17034"/><hi type="bold">31. covet earnestly--</hi>Greek, "emulously desire." Not in the spirit of discontented "coveting." The Spirit "divides to every man severally as He will" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.1">1Co 12:1</reference>); but this does not prevent men earnestly seeking, by prayer and watchfulness, and cultivation of their faculties, the greatest gifts. Beza explains, "Hold in the highest estimation"; which accords with the distinction in his view (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1">1Co 14:1</reference>) between "follow after charity--zealously esteem spiritual gifts"; also with (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.11">1Co 12:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.18">18</reference>) the sovereign will with which the Spirit distributes the gifts, precluding individuals from desiring gifts not vouchsafed to them. But see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1">1Co 14:1</reference>.<div eID="gen33705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the best gifts--</hi>Most of the oldest manuscripts read, "the greatest gifts."<div eID="gen33706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33707" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and yet--</hi>Greek, "and moreover." Besides recommending your zealous desire for the greatest gifts, I am about to show you a something still more excellent (literally, "a way most way-like") to desire, "the way of love" (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1">1Co 14:1</reference>). This love, or "charity," includes both "faith" and "hope" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.7">1Co 13:7</reference>), and bears the same fruits (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1-1Cor.13.13">1Co 13:1-13</reference>) as the ordinary and permanent fruits of the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.22-Gal.5.24">Ga 5:22-24</reference>). Thus "long-suffering," compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4">1Co 12:4</reference>; "faith," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.7">1Co 12:7</reference>; "joy," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.6">1Co 12:6</reference>; "meekness," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.5">1Co 12:5</reference>; "goodness," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.5">1Co 12:5</reference>; "gentleness," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4">1Co 12:4</reference> (the Greek is the same for "is kind"). It is the work of the Holy Spirit, and consists in love to God, on account of God's love in Christ to us, and as a consequence, love to man, especially to the brethren in Christ (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Ro 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.15.30">15:30</reference>). This is more to be desired than gifts (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.20">Lu 10:20</reference>). <chapter eID="1Cor.12"/>

entries.e7cac1d80ff2fb08251e8ab64df3298310ea43b9: <div eID="gen48111" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen48112" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen48113" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen48113" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen48112" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen48114" type="x-p"/> The apostle proceeds to the question of the Corinthians concerning spiritual gifts, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.1">1Cor 12:1</reference>. He calls to their remembrance their former state, and how they were brought out of it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.2">1Cor 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1Cor 12:3</reference>. Shows that there are diversities of gifts which proceed from the Spirit, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4">1Cor 12:4</reference>. Diversities of administrations which proceed from the Lord Jesus, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.5">1Cor 12:5</reference>. And diversities of operations which proceed from God, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.6">1Cor 12:6</reference>. What these gifts are, and how they are dispensed, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.7-1Cor.12.11">1Cor 12:7-11</reference>. Christ is the Head, and the Church his members; and this is pointed out under the similitude of the human body, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.12">1Cor 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.13">1Cor 12:13</reference>. The relation which the members of the body have to each other; and how necessary their mutual support, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.14-1Cor.12.26">1Cor 12:14-26</reference>. The members in the Church, or spiritual body, and their respective offices, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.27-1Cor.12.30">1Cor 12:27-30</reference>. We should earnestly covet the best gifts, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.31">1Cor 12:31</reference>. <div eID="gen48114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48115" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen48115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48116" type="x-p"/> Now concerning spiritual gifts - This was a subject about which they appear to have written to the apostle, and concerning which there were probably some contentions among them. The words περι των πνευματικων may as well be translated concerning spiritual persons, as spiritual gifts; and indeed the former agrees much better with the context. <div eID="gen48116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48117" type="x-p"/> I would not have you ignorant - I wish you fully to know whence all such gifts come, and for what end they are given, that each person may serve the Church in the capacity in which God has placed him, that there may be no misunderstandings and no schism in the body.
entries.7256c5d81b9b52e6bdab1cfb28aa785bd213eec8: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen48117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48118" type="x-p"/> Ye were Gentiles - Previously to your conversion to the Christian faith; ye were heathens, carried away, not guided by reason or truth, but hurried by your passions into a senseless worship, the chief part of which was calculated only to excite and gratify animal propensities. <div eID="gen48118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48119" type="x-p"/> Dumb idols - Though often supplicated, could never return an answer; so that not only the image could not speak, but the god or demon pretended to be represented by it could not speak: a full proof that an idol was nothing in the world.
entries.82ba9738b207aee89b2707d35e2c7b665a197c72: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen48119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48120" type="x-p"/> No man speaking by the Spirit of God - It was granted on all hands that there could be no religion without Divine inspiration, because God alone, could make his will known to men: hence heathenism pretended to this inspiration; Judaism had it in the law and the prophets; and it was the very essence of the Christian religion. The heathen priests and priestesses pretended to receive, by inspiration from their god, the answers which they gave to their votaries. And as far as the people believed their pretensions, so far they were led by their teaching. <div eID="gen48120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48121" type="x-p"/> Both Judaism and heathenism were full of expectations of a future teacher and deliverer; and to this person, especially among the Jews, the Spirit in all the prophets gave witness. This was the Anointed One, the Messiah who was manifested in the person of Jesus of Nazareth; and him the Jews rejected, though he proved his Divine mission both by his doctrines and his miracles. But as he did not come as they fancied he would - as a mighty secular conqueror, they not only rejected but blasphemed him; and persons among them professing to be spiritual men, and under the influence of the Spirit of God, did so. But as the Holy Spirit, through all the law and the prophets gave Testimony to the Messiah, and as Jesus proved himself to be the Christ both by his miracles and doctrines, no man under the inspiration of the Divine Spirit could say to him anathema - thou art a deceiver, and a person worthy of death, etc., as the Jews did: therefore the Jews were no longer under the inspiration of the Spirit of God. This appears to be the meaning of the apostle in this place. No man speaking by the Spirit, etc. <div eID="gen48121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48122" type="x-p"/> And that no man can say that Jesus is the Lord - Nor can we demonstrate this person to be the Messiah and the Savior of men, but by the Holy Ghost, enabling us to speak with divers tongues, to work miracles; he attesting the truth of our doctrines to them that hear, by enlightening their minds, changing their hearts, and filling them with the peace and love of God.
entries.de59d613d4afbc77e7f372195f4a41e8c10697ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen48122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48123" type="x-p"/> There are diversities of gifts - Χαρισματων· Gracious endowments, leading to miraculous results; such as the gift of prophecy, speaking different tongues, etc. And these all came by the extraordinary influences of the Holy Spirit.
entries.a00e4ce9d4a2c245997f1bbdeb9bb681f74a723d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen48123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48124" type="x-p"/> Differences of administrations - Διακονιων· Various offices in the Church, such as apostle, prophet, and teacher; under which were probably included bishop or presbyter, pastor, deacon, etc.; the qualifications for such offices, as well as the appointments themselves, coming immediately from the one Lord Jesus Christ.
entries.61a013157002c0f6663b77086adfe6925cfe7df0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen48124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48125" type="x-p"/> Diversities of operations - Ενεργηματων· Miraculous influences exerted on others; such as the expulsion of demons, inflicting extraordinary punishments, as in the case of Ananias and Sapphira, Elymas the sorcerer, etc., the healing of different diseases, raising the dead, etc.: all these proceeded from God the Father, as the fountain of all goodness and power, and the immediate dispenser of every good and perfect gift. <div eID="gen48125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48126" type="x-p"/> In the three preceding verses we find more than an indirect reference to the doctrine of the sacred Trinity. <div eID="gen48126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48127" type="x-p"/> Gifts are attributed to the Holy Spirit, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4">1Cor 12:4</reference>. <div eID="gen48127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48128" type="x-p"/> Administrations to the Lord Jesus, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.5">1Cor 12:5</reference>. <div eID="gen48128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48129" type="x-p"/> Operations to God the Father, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.6">1Cor 12:6</reference>. <div eID="gen48129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48130" type="x-p"/> He who may think this fanciful must account for the very evident distinctions here in some more satisfactory way.
entries.6331ced7fd182dc850f677aca4ea019e6934cbfd: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen48130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48131" type="x-p"/> The manifestation of the Spirit - Φανερωσις του Πνευματος. This is variably understood by the fathers; some of them rendering φανερωσις by illumination, others demonstration, and others operation. The apostle's meaning seems to be this: Whatever gifts God has bestowed, or in what various ways soever the Spirit of God may have manifested himself, it is all for the common benefit of the Church. God has given no gift to any man for his own private advantage, or exclusive profit. He has it for the benefit of others as well as for his own salvation.
entries.f1e3bfb7e1b9ffd1974d415538aa97b1f5586b6f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen48131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48132" type="x-p"/> Word of wisdom - In all these places I consider that the proper translation of λογος is doctrine, as in many other places of the New Testament. It is very difficult to say what is intended here by the different kinds of gifts mentioned by the apostle: they were probably all supernatural, and were necessary at that time only for the benefit of the Church. On the 8th, 9th, and 10th verses (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.8-1Cor.12.10">1Cor 12:8-10</reference>), much may be seen in Lightfoot, Whitby, Pearce, and others. <div eID="gen48132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48133" type="x-p"/> 1. By doctrine of wisdom we may understand, as Bp. Pearce and Dr. Whitby observe, the mystery of our redemption, in which the wisdom of God was most eminently conspicuous: see <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Cor 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10">1Cor 2:10</reference>; and which is called the manifold wisdom of God, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Eph 3:10</reference>. Christ, the great teacher of it, is called the wisdom of God, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.24">1Cor 1:24</reference>; and in him are said to be contained all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, <reference osisRef="Col.2.3">Col 2:3</reference>. The apostles to whom this doctrine was committed are called σοφοι, wise men; (<reference osisRef="Mat.23.34">Mat 23:34</reference>); and they are said to teach this Gospel according to the wisdom given them, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.15">2Pet 3:15</reference>. <div eID="gen48133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48134" type="x-p"/> 2. By the doctrine of knowledge we may understand either a knowledge of the types, etc., in the Old Testament; or what are termed mysteries; the calling of the Gentiles, the recalling of the Jews, the mystery of iniquity, of the beast, etc., and especially the mystical sense or meaning of the Old Testament, with all its types, rites, ceremonies, etc., etc. <div eID="gen48134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48135" type="x-p"/> 3. By faith, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.9">1Cor 12:9</reference>, we are to understand that miraculous faith by which they could remove mountains, <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.2">1Cor 13:2</reference>; or a peculiar impulse, as Dr: Whitby calls it, that came upon the apostles when any difficult matter was to be performed, which inwardly assured them that God's power would assist them in the performance of it. Others think that justifying faith, received by means of Gospel teaching, is what is intended. <div eID="gen48135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48136" type="x-p"/> 4. Gifts of healing simply refers to the power which at particular times the apostles received from the Holy Spirit to cure diseases; a power which was not always resident in them; for Paul could not cure Timothy, nor remove his own thorn in the flesh; because it was given only on extraordinary occasions, though perhaps more generally than many others. <div eID="gen48136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48137" type="x-p"/> 5. The working of miracles, ενεργηματα δυναμεων, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.10">1Cor 12:10</reference>. This seems to refer to the same class as the operations, ενεργηματων, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.6">1Cor 12:6</reference>, as the words are the same; and to signify those powers by which they were enabled at particular times to work miraculously on others; ejecting demons, inflicting punishments or judgments, as in the cases mentioned under <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.6">1Cor 12:6</reference>. It is a hendyadis for mighty operations. <div eID="gen48137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48138" type="x-p"/> 6. Prophecy. This seems to import two things: 1st, the predicting future events, such as then particularly concerned the state of the Church and the apostles; as the dearth foretold by Agabus, <reference osisRef="Act.11.28">Act 11:28</reference>; and the binding of St. Paul, and delivering him to the Romans, <reference osisRef="Act.21.10">Act 21:10</reference>, etc.; and St. Paul's foretelling his own shipwreck on Malta, <reference osisRef="Act.27.25">Act 27:25</reference>, etc. And 2ndly, as implying the faculty of teaching or expounding the Scriptures, which is also a common acceptation of the word. <div eID="gen48138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48139" type="x-p"/> 7. Discerning of spirits. A gift by which the person so privileged could discern a false miracle from a true one; or a pretender to inspiration from him who was made really partaker of the Holy Ghost. It probably extended also to the discernment of false professors from true ones, as appears in Peter in the case of Ananias and his wife. <div eID="gen48139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48140" type="x-p"/> 8. Divers kinds of tongues. Γενη γλωσσων, Different languages, which they had never learned, and which God gave them for the immediate instruction of people of different countries who attended their ministry. <div eID="gen48140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48141" type="x-p"/> 9. Interpretation of tongues. It was necessary that while one was speaking the deep things of God in a company where several were present who did not understand, though the majority did, there should be a person who could immediately interpret what was said to that part of the congregation that did not understand the language. This power to interpret was also an immediate gift of God's Spirit, and is classed here among the miracles.
entries.85942c9039e1751abd254f71df8f15670b93dd85: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen48141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48142" type="x-p"/> But all these worketh that one and the self-same Spirit - All these gifts are miraculously bestowed; they cannot be acquitted by human art or industry, the different languages excepted; but they were given in such a way, and in such circumstances, as sufficiently proved that they also were miraculous gifts.
entries.8b8075cbd6d915a33ad222ae114d03a5ac56f0a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen48142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48143" type="x-p"/> For as the body is one - Though the human body have many members, and though it be composed of a great variety of parts, yet it is but one entire system; every part and member being necessary to the integrity or completeness of the whole. <div eID="gen48143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48144" type="x-p"/> So also is Christ - That is, So is the Church the body of Christ, being composed of the different officers already mentioned, and especially those enumerated, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.28">1Cor 12:28</reference>, apostles, prophets, teachers, etc. It cannot be supposed that Christ is composed of many members, etc., and therefore the term Church must be understood, unless we suppose, which is not improbable, that the term Ὁ Χριστος, Christ, is used to express the Church, or whole body of Christian believers.
